claim: Mammalian glutamate transporters perform neurotransmitter reuptake from the synaptic cleft.
source: Mammalian glutamate transporters are crucial players in neuronal communication as they perform neurotransmitter reuptake from the synaptic cleft.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the function of mammalian glutamate transporters.

claim: Mammalian glutamate transporters recognize L-glutamate, L-aspartate, and D-aspartate.
source: Besides L-glutamate and L-aspartate, they also recognize D-aspartate, which might participate in mammalian neurotransmission and/or neuromodulation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the manuscript and established knowledge.

claim: D-aspartate might participate in mammalian neurotransmission and/or neuromodulation.
source: Besides L-glutamate and L-aspartate, they also recognize D-aspartate, which might participate in mammalian neurotransmission and/or neuromodulation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement indicated by the word 'might'.

claim: GltPh from Pyrococcus horikoshii and GltTk from Thermococcus kodakarensis are archaeal homologs that provide mechanistic insight into glutamate transport.
source: Much of the mechanistic insight in glutamate transport comes from studies of the archeal homologs GltPh from Pyrococcus horikoshii and GltTk from Thermococcus kodakarensis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: GltTk transports D-aspartate with identical Na+:substrate coupling stoichiometry as L-aspartate.
source: Here, we show that GltTk transports D-aspartate with identical Na+: substrate coupling stoichiometry as L-aspartate, and that the affinities (Kd and Km) for the two substrates are similar.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The affinities (Kd and Km) of GltTk for D-aspartate and L-aspartate are similar.
source: Here, we show that GltTk transports D-aspartate with identical Na+: substrate coupling stoichiometry as L-aspartate, and that the affinities (Kd and Km) for the two substrates are similar.
evidence: This is supported by ITC and transport assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A crystal structure of GltTk with bound D-aspartate was determined at 2.8 Å resolution.
source: We determined a crystal structure of GltTk with bound D-aspartate at 2.8 Å resolution.
evidence: This is directly supported by the crystallographic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: D-aspartate is accommodated in the GltTk binding site with only minor rearrangements compared to L-aspartate.
source: Comparison of the L- and D-aspartate bound GltTk structures revealed that D-aspartate is accommodated with only minor rearrangements in the structure of the binding site.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The structure explains how the geometrically different molecules L- and D-aspartate are recognized and transported by the protein in the same way.
source: The structure explains how the geometrically different molecules L- and D-aspartate are recognized and transported by the protein in the same way.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data presented.

claim: EAATs are secondary transporters that couple glutamate uptake to co-transport of three sodium ions and one proton and counter-transport of one potassium ion.
source: EAATs are secondary transporters that couple glutamate uptake to co-transport of three sodium ions and one proton and counter-transport of one potassium ion (Levy et al., 1998; Owe et al., 2006; Zerangue and Kavanaugh, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: EAATs transport L-glutamate, L- and D-aspartate with similar affinity.
source: EAATs transport L-glutamate, L- and D-aspartate with similar affinity (Arriza et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: D-aspartate is considered as a putative mammalian neurotransmitter and/or neuromodulator.
source: D-aspartate is considered as a putative mammalian neurotransmitter and/or neuromodulator (Brown et al., 2007; D'Aniello et al., 2011; Spinelli et al., 2006) (reviewed in D'Aniello, 2007; Genchi, 2017; Ota et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies and reviews.

claim: L-aspartate is proposed to have a role as a neurotransmitter, but this is still a matter of debate.
source: Such a role is also proposed for L-aspartate (Cavallero et al., 2009), however this is still a matter of debate (Herring et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations indicating both support and debate.

claim: Both D-aspartate and L-aspartate stereoisomers bind to and activate N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs).
source: Both stereoisomers bind to and activate N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) (Patneau and Mayer, 1990) and might be involved in learning and memory processes (reviewed in Errico et al., 2018; Errico and Usiello, 2017; Katane and Homma, 2011; Ota et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: D-aspartate and L-aspartate might be involved in learning and memory processes.
source: Both stereoisomers bind to and activate N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) (Patneau and Mayer, 1990) and might be involved in learning and memory processes (reviewed in Errico et al., 2018; Errico and Usiello, 2017; Katane and Homma, 2011; Ota et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by review citations.

claim: It is well established that EAATs take up D-aspartate.
source: Although it is well established that EAATs take up D-aspartate (Arriza et al., 1994; Gundersen et al., 1993), structural insight in the binding mode of the enantiomer is lacking.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Structural insight in the binding mode of D-aspartate to EAATs was lacking prior to this study.
source: Although it is well established that EAATs take up D-aspartate (Arriza et al., 1994; Gundersen et al., 1993), structural insight in the binding mode of the enantiomer is lacking.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of prior structural data.

claim: GltPh and GltTk are the best structurally characterized members of the glutamate transporter family.
source: The best structurally characterized members of the glutamate transporter family are the archeal homologs GltPh and GltTk (Akyuz et al., 2015; Boudker et al., 2007; Guskov et al., 2016; Jensen et al., 2013; Reyes et al., 2013; Reyes et al., 2009; Scopelliti et al., 2018; Verdon et al., 2014; Verdon and Boudker, 2012; Yernool et al., 2004), which share 32–36% sequence identity with eukaryotic EAATs (Jensen et al., 2013; Slotboom et al., 1999; Yernool et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to structural studies.

claim: GltPh and GltTk share 32–36% sequence identity with eukaryotic EAATs.
source: The best structurally characterized members of the glutamate transporter family are the archeal homologs GltPh and GltTk (Akyuz et al., 2015; Boudker et al., 2007; Guskov et al., 2016; Jensen et al., 2013; Reyes et al., 2013; Reyes et al., 2009; Scopelliti et al., 2018; Verdon et al., 2014; Verdon and Boudker, 2012; Yernool et al., 2004), which share 32–36% sequence identity with eukaryotic EAATs (Jensen et al., 2013; Slotboom et al., 1999; Yernool et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: GltPh and GltTk are highly selective for aspartate over glutamate.
source: In contrast to EAATs, GltPh and GltTk are highly selective for aspartate over glutamate, and couple uptake only to co-transport of three sodium ions (Boudker et al., 2007; Groeneveld and Slotboom, 2010; Guskov et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: GltPh and GltTk couple uptake only to co-transport of three sodium ions.
source: In contrast to EAATs, GltPh and GltTk are highly selective for aspartate over glutamate, and couple uptake only to co-transport of three sodium ions (Boudker et al., 2007; Groeneveld and Slotboom, 2010; Guskov et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The amino acid residues in the substrate-binding sites of mammalian and prokaryotic glutamate transporters are highly conserved.
source: Despite these differences, the amino acid residues in the substrate-binding sites of mammalian and prokaryotic glutamate transporters are highly conserved (Boudker et al., 2007; Jensen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The first structures of human members of the glutamate transporter family showed that the substrate-binding sites are highly similar among homologs.
source: The first structures of human members of the glutamate transporter family (Canul-Tec et al., 2017; Garaeva et al., 2018), showed that the substrate-binding sites are indeed highly similar among homologs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies and reference to a figure.

claim: The crystal structure of GltTk with D-aspartate was obtained in the outward-facing state.
source: The crystal structure was obtained in the outward-facing state with the substrate oriented in a very similar mode as L-aspartate, showing that the two enantiomers bind almost identically regardless of the mirrored spatial arrangement of functional groups around the chiral Cα atom.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: D-aspartate is oriented in a very similar mode as L-aspartate in the GltTk binding site.
source: The crystal structure was obtained in the outward-facing state with the substrate oriented in a very similar mode as L-aspartate, showing that the two enantiomers bind almost identically regardless of the mirrored spatial arrangement of functional groups around the chiral Cα atom.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The two enantiomers D-aspartate and L-aspartate bind almost identically regardless of the mirrored spatial arrangement of functional groups around the chiral Cα atom.
source: The crystal structure was obtained in the outward-facing state with the substrate oriented in a very similar mode as L-aspartate, showing that the two enantiomers bind almost identically regardless of the mirrored spatial arrangement of functional groups around the chiral Cα atom.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: The affinity of GltTk for D-aspartate is strongly dependent on the concentration of sodium ions.
source: The affinity of the transporter for D-aspartate was strongly dependent on the concentration of sodium, similar to what has been reported for L-aspartate binding to GltPh and GltTk (Boudker et al., 2007; Hänelt et al., 2015; Jensen et al., 2013; Reyes et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data presented in the manuscript.

claim: At 500 mM sodium concentration, the Kd of GltTk for D-aspartate is 374 ± 30 nM.
source: At high sodium concentration (500 mM), the Kd values of GltTk for D- and L-aspartate binding level off to 374 ± 30 nM and 62 ± 3 nM, respectively.
evidence: This is directly supported by ITC measurements.

claim: At 500 mM sodium concentration, the Kd of GltTk for L-aspartate is 62 ± 3 nM.
source: At high sodium concentration (500 mM), the Kd values of GltTk for D- and L-aspartate binding level off to 374 ± 30 nM and 62 ± 3 nM, respectively.
evidence: This is directly supported by ITC measurements.

claim: The ΔH values for binding of both D-aspartate and L-aspartate to GltTk were favorable.
source: The ΔH values for binding of both substrates were favorable, with a more negative value of ~1 kcal mol−1 for L-aspartate, indicating a better binding geometry for L- than for D-aspartate.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data.

claim: L-aspartate has a more negative ΔH value by ~1 kcal mol−1 compared to D-aspartate, indicating a better binding geometry.
source: The ΔH values for binding of both substrates were favorable, with a more negative value of ~1 kcal mol−1 for L-aspartate, indicating a better binding geometry for L- than for D-aspartate.
evidence: This is an inference based on ITC data.

claim: For both D-aspartate and L-aspartate, the ΔS contribution to binding was unfavorable.
source: For both substrates, the ΔS contribution was unfavorable (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data in Table 1.

claim: Binding of both D-aspartate and L-aspartate to GltTk is coupled to the binding of three sodium ions.
source: When plotting the observed Kd values for L- and D-aspartate against the sodium concentration (on logarithmic scales), the slopes of both curves in the lower limit of the sodium concentration are close to −3, indicating that binding of both compounds is coupled to the binding of three sodium ions (Boudker et al., 2007; Lolkema and Slotboom, 2015) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data analysis and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The Km for D-aspartate transport by GltTk is 1.1 ± 0.11 μM at 100 mM sodium concentration.
source: The Km for transport was 1.1 ± 0.11 μM at a sodium concentration of 100 mM (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is directly supported by transport assay data.

claim: The Km for L-aspartate transport by GltTk is 0.75 ± 0.17 μM at 100 mM sodium concentration.
source: This value is comparable to the Km for L-aspartate uptake under the same conditions (0.75 ± 0.17 μM).
evidence: This is directly supported by transport assay data.

claim: D-aspartate is most likely symported with three sodium ions by GltTk.
source: From these data, we conclude that D-aspartate is most likely symported with three sodium ions.
evidence: This is an inference based on equilibrium potential measurements.

claim: The equilibrium potentials for experiments using D-aspartate and L-aspartate were identical.
source: The equilibrium potentials for the experiments using D- and L-aspartate were identical, showing that the two stereoisomers use the same coupling stoichiometry.
evidence: This is supported by flux measurement data.

claim: D-aspartate and L-aspartate use the same coupling stoichiometry in GltTk.
source: The equilibrium potentials for the experiments using D- and L-aspartate were identical, showing that the two stereoisomers use the same coupling stoichiometry.
evidence: This is an inference based on equilibrium potential measurements.

claim: The GltTk structure with D-aspartate is highly similar to previously described GltTk and GltPh structures with the transport domains in the outward-oriented occluded state.
source: The obtained structure is highly similar to the previously described GltTk and GltPh structures with the transport domains in the outward-oriented occluded state.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: D-aspartate and L-aspartate form almost identical hydrogen bonding networks with conserved amino acid residues of the substrate-binding site in GltTk.
source: Despite the impossibility to superimpose two enantiomers, D- and L-aspartate are capable of forming almost identical hydrogen bonding networks with conserved amino acid residues of the substrate-binding site (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and Figure 2C.

claim: There are only small changes in the positions of the Cα atoms and Cβ carboxyl groups between D-aspartate and L-aspartate binding due to constitutional differences.
source: There are only small changes in the positions of the Cα atoms and Cβ carboxyl groups due to the constitutional differences.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The small structural differences between D-aspartate and L-aspartate binding lead to only minor changes in the interaction network, consistent with comparable Kd and ΔH values.
source: However, this divergence leads to only minor changes in the interaction network, consistent with the comparable Kd and ΔH values determined by ITC (Table 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and thermodynamic data.

claim: The GltTk model contains one protein molecule in the asymmetric unit with the substrate present in each protomer of the homotrimer.
source: The model contains one protein molecule in the asymmetric unit with the substrate present in each protomer of the homotrimer.
evidence: This is a description of the crystal structure.

claim: Three peaks of electron density located at the same positions as three sodium ions in the GltTk complex with L-aspartate most probably correspond to sodium ions.
source: Three peaks of electron density (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 2) located at the same positions as three sodium ions in the GltTk complex with L-aspartate (Guskov et al., 2016) most probably correspond to sodium ions, consistent with a 3:1 Na+: D-aspartate coupling stoichiometry (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: This is an inference based on electron density maps and comparison with previous structures.

claim: Most proteins selectively bind a single stereoisomer of their substrates.
source: Most proteins selectively bind a single stereoisomer of their substrates (for a review see Nguyen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Some proteins are able to bind different stereoisomers of a ligand, which is believed to be possible due to different binding modes.
source: On the other hand, some proteins are able to bind different stereoisomers of a ligand, which is believed to be possible due to different binding modes, because enantiomers cannot be superimposed in the three-dimensional space and thus cannot interact with the binding site identically.
evidence: This is established knowledge about protein-ligand interactions.

claim: Enantiomers cannot be superimposed in three-dimensional space and thus cannot interact with the binding site identically.
source: On the other hand, some proteins are able to bind different stereoisomers of a ligand, which is believed to be possible due to different binding modes, because enantiomers cannot be superimposed in the three-dimensional space and thus cannot interact with the binding site identically.
evidence: This is established knowledge about stereochemistry.

claim: Based on three- and four-point attachment models, it has been suggested that stereoisomers can bind in the same site but with significant differences.
source: Based on three- and four-point attachment models (Easson and Stedman, 1933; Mesecar and Koshland, 2000; Ogston, 1948) it has been suggested that stereoisomers can bind in the same site but with significant differences.
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical models.

claim: The hypothesis that stereoisomers can bind in the same site but with significant differences was supported by crystal structures of enzymes with different enantiomeric substrates.
source: This hypothesis was supported by crystal structures of enzymes with different enantiomeric substrates (Brem et al., 2016; Sabini et al., 2008), including enantiomeric amino acids (Aghaiypour et al., 2001; Bharath et al., 2012; Driggers et al., 2016; Temperini et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The binding poses of enantiomers in some enzymes are remarkably similar, for instance in aspartate/glutamate racemase EcL-DER, where active site forms pseudo-mirror symmetry.
source: In contrast, the binding poses of enantiomers in some other enzymes are remarkably similar, for instance in aspartate/glutamate racemase EcL-DER, where active site forms pseudo-mirror symmetry (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a structural study.

claim: GltTk is the first amino acid transporter for which the binding of enantiomeric substrates has been characterized.
source: To our knowledge GltTk is the first amino acid transporter for which the binding of enantiomeric substrates has been characterized.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: AgcS is the only other transporter for which structures have been determined in the presence of D- and L-substrates.
source: The only other transporter for which structures have been determined in the presence of D- and L-substrates is the sodium-alanine symporter AgcS.
evidence: This is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: In AgcS, limited resolution prevented determination of the absolute orientation of bound enantiomers.
source: However, in that case, limited resolution prevented determination of the absolute orientation of bound enantiomers (Ma et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a structural study.

claim: In the substrate-binding site of GltTk, L- and D-aspartate take similar poses leading to almost identical networks of contacts.
source: In the substrate-binding site of GltTk, L- and D-aspartate take similar poses leading to almost identical networks of contacts.
evidence: This is supported by structural data.

claim: Mirror imaged substrates inevitably have differences in angles between donors and acceptors of hydrogen bonds.
source: Since mirror imaged substrates inevitably have differences in angles between donors and acceptors of hydrogen bonds, the binding affinities are not identical, with 4–6 times higher Kd of the GltTk-D-aspartate complex in comparison with L-aspartate (Table 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about stereochemistry.

claim: The Kd of the GltTk-D-aspartate complex is 4–6 times higher than for L-aspartate.
source: Since mirror imaged substrates inevitably have differences in angles between donors and acceptors of hydrogen bonds, the binding affinities are not identical, with 4–6 times higher Kd of the GltTk-D-aspartate complex in comparison with L-aspartate (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data in Table 1.

claim: Similar differences in binding affinities between D-aspartate and L-aspartate were found for the GltPh homologue.
source: Similar differences in binding affinities between these enantiomers were also found for the GltPh homologue (Boudker et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The higher Kd values for D-aspartate might be explained by a higher dissociation rate (koff) compared to L-aspartate.
source: The higher Kd values for the D-aspartate enantiomer might be explained by a higher dissociation rate (koff) in comparison with L-aspartate, that was shown in kinetic studies of sodium and aspartate binding on ﻿GltPh (Ewers et al., 2013; Hänelt et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to kinetic studies.

claim: The binding of D-aspartate to GltTk is not accompanied by a loss of sodium binding sites.
source: Although the affinity for D-aspartate is lower than for L-aspartate, the binding of D-aspartate is not accompanied by a loss of sodium binding sites, which is in line with the observation that none of the sodium binding sites are directly coordinated by the substrate L-aspartate.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data.

claim: None of the sodium binding sites in GltTk are directly coordinated by the substrate L-aspartate.
source: Although the affinity for D-aspartate is lower than for L-aspartate, the binding of D-aspartate is not accompanied by a loss of sodium binding sites, which is in line with the observation that none of the sodium binding sites are directly coordinated by the substrate L-aspartate.
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge from previous studies.

claim: The mechanism of D- and L-aspartate transport in GltTk is most probably identical.
source: Altogether our data suggest that the mechanism of D- and L-aspartate transport in GltTk is most probably identical.
evidence: This is an inference based on all the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mammalian glutamate transporters take up D-aspartate, L-glutamate and L-aspartate with similar micromolar affinity.
source: Mammalian glutamate transporters take up D-aspartate, L-glutamate and L-aspartate with similar micromolar affinity, but have significantly lower affinity (millimolar) for D-glutamate (Arriza et al., 1997; Arriza et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mammalian glutamate transporters have significantly lower affinity (millimolar) for D-glutamate.
source: Mammalian glutamate transporters take up D-aspartate, L-glutamate and L-aspartate with similar micromolar affinity, but have significantly lower affinity (millimolar) for D-glutamate (Arriza et al., 1997; Arriza et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The extra methylene group in D-glutamate compared to D-aspartate could cause steric clashes within the binding site of EAATs.
source: It seems that the extra methylene group in D-glutamate compared to D-aspartate could cause sterical clashes within the binding site (Figure 2﻿— Figure 2—figure supplement 3), which might affect affinity of binding.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural modeling shown in a figure.

claim: Steric clashes from the extra methylene group in D-glutamate might affect affinity of binding to EAATs.
source: It seems that the extra methylene group in D-glutamate compared to D-aspartate could cause sterical clashes within the binding site (Figure 2﻿— Figure 2—figure supplement 3), which might affect affinity of binding.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural modeling.

claim: The GltTk structures with D- and L-aspartate can be aligned with Cα-RMSD = 0.38 Å for the three transport domains.
source: The GltTk structures with D- and L-aspartate can be aligned with Cα-RMSD = 0.38 Å for the three transport domains.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure from structural alignment.

claim: All side chains involved in L-aspartate binding are highly conserved and identical in GltTk and EAAT1.
source: All side chains involved in L-aspartate binding are highly conserved and identical in GltTk (PDB code 5E9S; L-aspartate is shown as green sticks) and EAAT1 (PDB code 5LM4; pale cyan).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: D-glutamate might clash with highly conservative T402 and R479 of EAAT1 that both coordinate Cβ carboxyl group of L-aspartate.
source: The model shows that D-glutamate might clash with highly conservative T402 (NMDGT motif of TMS7; T317 in GltTk) and R479 (TMS8; R401 in GltTk) of EAAT1 that both coordinate Cβ carboxyl group of L-aspartate.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural modeling shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: L-glutamate might be placed with orientation similar to L-aspartate in EAAT1, preventing clashes.
source: In contrast L-glutamate might be placed with orientation similar to L-aspartate, preventing clashes.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural modeling.

claim: At 300 mM NaCl, the Kd of GltTk for L-aspartate is 0.12 ± 0.04 µM.
source: L-aspartate/300 mM NaCl	0.12 ± 0.04
evidence: This is directly supported by ITC data in Table 1.

claim: At 300 mM NaCl, the Kd of GltTk for D-aspartate is 0.47 ± 0.17 µM.
source: D-aspartate/300 mM NaCl	0.47 ± 0.17
evidence: This is directly supported by ITC data in Table 1.

claim: At 75 mM NaCl, the Kd of GltTk for L-aspartate is 1.04 ± 0.39 µM.
source: L-aspartate/75 mM NaCl	1.04 ± 0.39
evidence: This is directly supported by ITC data in Table 1.

claim: At 75 mM NaCl, the Kd of GltTk for D-aspartate is 5.66 ± 1.59 µM.
source: D-aspartate/75 mM NaCl	5.66 ± 1.59
evidence: This is directly supported by ITC data in Table 1.

claim: The crystal structure of GltTk with D-aspartate has space group P3221.
source: Space group	P3221
evidence: This is crystallographic data from Table 2.

claim: The crystal structure of GltTk with D-aspartate has unit cell dimensions a = 116.55 Å, b = 116.55 Å, c = 314.77 Å.
evidence: This is crystallographic data from Table 2.

claim: The crystal structure of GltTk with D-aspartate was refined to Rwork/Rfree values of 23.4%/27.2%.
source: Rwork/Rfree (%)s	23.4/27.2
evidence: This is crystallographic refinement data from Table 2.

claim: L-aspartate binds to GltTk only if sodium ions are present.
source: It was shown that L-aspartate binds to GltTk only if sodium ions are present, and the protein purified in absence of sodium ions is in the apo state (Jensen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The protein purified in absence of sodium ions is in the apo state.
source: It was shown that L-aspartate binds to GltTk only if sodium ions are present, and the protein purified in absence of sodium ions is in the apo state (Jensen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.
